claim: COVID-19 CG (covidcg.org) is an open resource for tracking SARS-CoV-2 single-nucleotide variations (SNVs), lineages, and clades using the virus genomes on the GISAID database while filtering by location, date, gene, and mutation of interest.
source: COVID-19 CG (covidcg.org) is an open resource for tracking SARS-CoV-2 single-nucleotide variations (SNVs), lineages, and clades using the virus genomes on the GISAID database while filtering by location, date, gene, and mutation of interest.
evidence: This is a description of the tool's functionality and data source as stated in the abstract.

claim: There were 400,000+ virus genomes as of February 2020 on the GISAID database.
source: Since the beginning of the pandemic, SARS-CoV-2 genomic data has been accumulating at an unprecedented rate (400,000+ virus genomes as of February 2020 on the GISAID database) (Elbe and Buckland-Merrett, 2017; Shu and McCauley, 2017).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the number of genomes in GISAID, supported by citations to the GISAID database papers.

claim: Numerous countries have mobilized to sequence thousands of SARS-CoV-2 genomes upon the occurrence of local outbreaks, collectively and consistently contributing more than 20,000 genomes per month.
source: Numerous countries have mobilized to sequence thousands of SARS-CoV-2 genomes upon the occurrence of local outbreaks, collectively and consistently contributing more than 20,000 genomes per month (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B which shows sequencing data over time.

claim: There has been a steady increase in the number of variants with more than six nonsynonymous mutations compared to the WIV04 reference.
source: It is important to note that, despite the slow accumulation of potentially functional (nonsynonymous) mutations, there has been a steady increase in the number of variants with more than six nonsynonymous mutations compared to the WIV04 reference, an early genome of SARS-CoV-2 that was sampled in Wuhan in December 2019 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C showing the increase in variants with multiple nonsynonymous mutations.

claim: WIV04 is an early genome of SARS-CoV-2 that was sampled in Wuhan in December 2019.
source: It is important to note that, despite the slow accumulation of potentially functional (nonsynonymous) mutations, there has been a steady increase in the number of variants with more than six nonsynonymous mutations compared to the WIV04 reference, an early genome of SARS-CoV-2 that was sampled in Wuhan in December 2019 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the WIV04 reference genome's origin.

claim: Several countries and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) have recognized how critical it is to collect SARS-CoV-2 genomic data to support contact tracing efforts and to inform public health decisions.
source: Indeed, several countries and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) have recognized how critical it is to collect SARS-CoV-2 genomic data to support contact tracing efforts and to inform public health decisions – these are paramount to the re-opening of countries and inter-regional travel (Collins, 2020; Gudbjartsson et al., 2020; Oude Munnink et al., 2020; Virological, 2020; Rockett et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant publications.

claim: COVID-19 CG is a performant, interactive, and fully scalable web application that tracks SARS-CoV-2 single-nucleotide variants (SNVs), lineages, and clades without sub-sampling.
source: To address this challenge, we built COVID-19 CoV Genetics (COVID-19 CG, covidcg.org), a performant, interactive, and fully scalable web application that tracks SARS-CoV-2 single-nucleotide variants (SNVs), lineages, and clades without sub-sampling.
evidence: This is a description of the tool's technical characteristics as stated by the authors.

claim: COVID-19 CG is a free, open access interface that allows users to adapt analyses according to their dates and locations of interest.
source: COVID-19 CG is a free, open access interface that allows users to adapt analyses according to their dates and locations of interest (Figure 1A,B; data processing workflow in Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim describes the tool's accessibility and functionality, with reference to figures showing the interface.

claim: As of December 2020, an S477N mutation in the receptor binding domain (RBD) has become dominant in Australia (69% of Australian SARS-CoV-2 genotypes, all time).
source: For instance, as of December 2020, an S477N mutation in the receptor binding domain (RBD) has become dominant in Australia (69% of Australian SARS-CoV-2 genotypes, all time) although it constitutes less than 6% of SARS-CoV-2 genotypes globally (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a specific data point about mutation frequency in Australia, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: The S477N mutation constitutes less than 6% of SARS-CoV-2 genotypes globally as of December 2020.
source: For instance, as of December 2020, an S477N mutation in the receptor binding domain (RBD) has become dominant in Australia (69% of Australian SARS-CoV-2 genotypes, all time) although it constitutes less than 6% of SARS-CoV-2 genotypes globally (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a specific data point about global mutation frequency, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: An RBD N439K mutation not found in Ireland prior to July was present in 42% of the genomes collected mid-July through September, peaking in August and gradually fading after.
source: SNV frequency in a given region can also shift over time, for example, an RBD N439K mutation not found in Ireland prior to July was present in 42% of the genomes collected mid-July through September, peaking in August and gradually fading after (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a specific observation about temporal changes in mutation frequency in Ireland, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: A rare RBD S477N mutation, which was found in only 1% of the Australian SARS-CoV-2 sequences before June, has constituted 84% of the sequenced June through December genomes.
source: Another rare RBD S477N mutation, which was found in only 1% of the Australian SARS-CoV-2 sequences before June, has constituted 84% of the sequenced June through December genomes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a specific observation about temporal changes in mutation frequency in Australia, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: Regeneron is developing therapeutic antibodies that specifically target the SARS-CoV-2 spike RBD.
source: This geographical and temporal variation is important to incorporate into the design and testing of therapeutic antibodies (such as those under development as therapeutics by Regeneron that specifically target the SARS-CoV-2 spike RBD), as well as mRNA or recombinant protein-based vaccines.
evidence: This is stated as an example of therapeutic antibodies in development.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Baum et al., 2020 study.

evidence: This is a statement about the conclusions drawn by Baum et al.

claim: A common G29140T SNV was found in 22.3% of samples from Madera County, California.
source: A recent preprint alerted us to the finding that a common G29140T SNV, found in 22.3% of the study's samples from Madera County, California, was adversely affecting SARS-CoV-2 detection by the NIID_2019-nCoV_N_F2 diagnostic primer used at their sequencing center; the single SNV caused a ~ 30-fold drop in the quantity of amplicon produced by the NIID_2019-nCov_N_F2/R2 primer pair (Vanaerschot et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the Vanaerschot et al., 2020 preprint.

claim: The G29140T SNV was adversely affecting SARS-CoV-2 detection by the NIID_2019-nCoV_N_F2 diagnostic primer.
source: A recent preprint alerted us to the finding that a common G29140T SNV, found in 22.3% of the study's samples from Madera County, California, was adversely affecting SARS-CoV-2 detection by the NIID_2019-nCoV_N_F2 diagnostic primer used at their sequencing center; the single SNV caused a ~ 30-fold drop in the quantity of amplicon produced by the NIID_2019-nCov_N_F2/R2 primer pair (Vanaerschot et al., 2020).

claim: There are SARS-CoV-2 variants in several countries with a C29144T mutation at the very 3' end of the NIID_2019-nCoV_N_F2 primer.
source: We used COVID-19 CG to detect other SNVs that could impact the use of this primer pair, discovering that there are SARS-CoV-2 variants in several countries with a different C29144T mutation at the very 3' end of the same NIID_2019-nCoV_N_F2 primer (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis using COVID-19 CG, supported by Figure 3A.

claim: At least 10 other primer pairs could potentially be at risk in different geographical regions due to SNVs that appear proximal to the 3' ends of primers.
source: We found that at least 10 other primer pairs could potentially be at risk in different geographical regions due to SNVs that appear proximal to the 3' ends of primers (Figure 3B–K): China-CDC-N-F and R; NIH, Thailand, WH-NIC N-F; US CDC 2019-nCoV-N1-R; US CDC 2019-nCoV-N2-F; ARTIC-V3_nCoV-2019_11_RIGHT; ARTIC-V3_nCoV-2019_13_LEFT; ARTIC-V3_nCoV-2019_34_LEFT; ARTIC-V3_nCoV-2019_39_LEFT (note that the ARTIC primers are used for nanopore sequencing; Tyson et al., 2020); WHO N_Sarbarco_R1; and Institut Pasteur, Paris 12759Rv.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis using COVID-19 CG, supported by Figure 3B-K.

claim: ARTIC primers are used for nanopore sequencing.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 spike S477N mutation was first detected globally in a single sample of lineage B.1.1.25 that was collected on March 19, 2020, in Victoria, Australia.
source: Globally, the S477N mutation was first detected in a single sample of lineage B.1.1.25 that was collected on March 19, 2020, in Victoria, Australia, and became the dominant SARS-CoV-2 variant in the region between June and September (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a specific observation from the genomic data, supported by Figure 5B.

claim: The S477N mutation became the dominant SARS-CoV-2 variant in Australia between June and September 2020.
source: Globally, the S477N mutation was first detected in a single sample of lineage B.1.1.25 that was collected on March 19, 2020, in Victoria, Australia, and became the dominant SARS-CoV-2 variant in the region between June and September (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a specific observation from the genomic data, supported by Figure 5B.

claim: The set of SNVs that co-occur with the S477N mutation in Australia are different from the set of co-occurring SNVs in the United Kingdom.
source: In particular, the set of SNVs that co-occur with the S477N mutation in Australia (all time, as well as prior to May 2020 before the most recent outbreak) are different from the set of co-occurring SNVs in the United Kingdom (Figure 5C) — suggesting that the S477N mutation occurred separately in the Australian and the UK lineages.
evidence: This is a specific observation from the genomic data, supported by Figure 5C.

claim: The S477N mutation occurred separately in the Australian and the UK lineages.
source: In particular, the set of SNVs that co-occur with the S477N mutation in Australia (all time, as well as prior to May 2020 before the most recent outbreak) are different from the set of co-occurring SNVs in the United Kingdom (Figure 5C) — suggesting that the S477N mutation occurred separately in the Australian and the UK lineages.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different co-occurring SNVs in Australia and the UK.

claim: Sequences meeting any of the following criteria are filtered out: present on NextStrain's exclusion list, genomes from non-humans, genome length less than 29,700 nt, or >5% ambiguous base calls.
source: Based on best practices, we filter out sequences meeting any of the following criteria: (1) present on the NextStrain's exclusion list (https://github.com/nextstrain/ncov/blob/master/defaults/exclude.txt; Hadfield et al., 2018), (2) genomes from non-humans (animals, environmental samples, etc.), (3) genome length less than 29,700 nt, or (4) >5% ambiguous base calls.
evidence: This is a description of the filtering methodology, supported by citation to best practices.

source: SNVs and insertions/deletions (indels) at the nucleotide and amino acid level are determined using bowtie2 by aligning each sequence to the WIV04 reference sequence (WIV04 is a high quality December 2019 genome that is 100% identical to the other commonly used publicly available SARS-CoV-2 genome reference Wuhan-Hu-1/NC_045512.2, excepting the length of the poly(A) tail).
evidence: This is a description of the SNV determination methodology.
